content: The recommended dosage of nitazoxanide for treating intestinal amebiasis varies by age group. For individuals aged 12 years and older, the dosage is 500 mg taken orally every 12 hours for three days. For children aged 4 to 11 years, the dosage is 10 mL (200 mg) orally every 12 hours for three days. For children aged 1 to 3 years, the dosage is 5 mL (100 mg) orally every 12 hours for three days. The safety and efficacy of nitazoxanide in children under 1 year of age have not been established. Nitazoxanide has potential drug interactions with several medications. It may increase the effects of certain drugs, such as baricitinib, by reducing their elimination, or enhance immunosuppressive effects when combined with drugs like axicabtagene ciloleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, or lisocabtagene maraleucel, increasing the risk of infection. In such cases, alternative drugs should be considered. Nitazoxanide can also increase the levels of drugs like phenytoin, valproic acid, and tacrolimus through plasma protein binding competition, necessitating caution and close monitoring. Additionally, coadministration with strong organic anion transporter 3 (OAT3) inhibitors is not recommended. Common side effects of nitazoxanide include headache (1%), abdominal pain (8%), diarrhea (2%), nausea (3%), vomiting (1%), and chromaturia (2%). Other potential adverse effects include increased ALT levels, anorexia, increased appetite, elevated creatinine, dizziness, fever, flatulence, malaise, pruritus, and skin rash. Rarely, hypersensitivity reactions may occur. The safety and efficacy of nitazoxanide in HIV-positive or immunodeficient patients, as well as those with hepatic or renal impairment, remain unknown, and caution is advised in these populations. Nitazoxanide should be taken with food. The suspension can be stored at room temperature for up to 7 days after reconstitution, after which any unused portion must be discarded. Children aged 11 years or younger should use the liquid form, as the safety of tablets in this age group has not been established. During pregnancy, nitazoxanide should only be used when clearly needed, as there is no data on its effects in pregnant women. Animal studies have not shown teratogenicity or fetotoxicity at doses significantly higher than the maximum recommended human dose. Breastfeeding mothers should weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against the potential risks to the infant from the medication or the underlying maternal condition. If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is close to the time of the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. Nitazoxanide should be stored at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and not in the bathroom. Unused medication should be properly discarded when expired or no longer needed. In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or a poison control center. This medication has been prescribed for your current condition only and should not be shared with others. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this medication and its use in your specific health situation.
